Part I — Finite Systems · Chapter 1. The Qubit · Lecture 1

The qubit

Objectives

A quantum system is given by its states, its observables, a Hamiltonian that moves the states, and a rule for the probabilities of readings and the state after a reading. This lecture builds all four for the simplest system, a quantum bit, starting from silver atoms in a magnet. The states are the points of a sphere, and the Hamiltonian turns the sphere.

1.1 Silver atoms and two magnets

Silver atoms from an oven pass through a Stern–Gerlach magnet, whose field is strong at one pole and weak at the other, and land on a screen. The uneven field pushes on the atom’s magnetic moment, the vector that measures how the atom responds to a magnetic field. The screen shows two separated beams (Figure 1.1; Sakurai and Napolitano, Figs 1.1–1.2). They correspond to the two readings of the atom’s intrinsic angular momentum, its spin, along the magnet’s direction. This lecture is the theory of the spin alone. We record the two readings as +1+1+1 and −1-1−1.

Keep only the atoms that read +1+1+1 in a magnet along zzz. Between the magnets the atoms fly through no field. Three facts describe what happens next (Figure 1.2), and this lecture will explain them.

(F1) A repeated reading repeats.

A second magnet along zzz reads +1+1+1 for all of them.

(F2) Probabilities vary smoothly.

A second magnet turned through an angle θ\thetaθ still has only two possible readings, +1+1+1 and −1-1−1. The fraction of atoms reading +1+1+1 is cos⁡2(θ/2)\cos^2(\theta/2)cos2(θ/2), and the fraction reading −1-1−1 is sin⁡2(θ/2)\sin^2(\theta/2)sin2(θ/2).

(F3) A reading changes the state.

Keep the atoms that read +1+1+1 along xxx (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2θ=π/2), and send them through a magnet along zzz. Half of them now read −1-1−1.

These fractions are the limits that measured frequencies approach.

No three-dimensional vector with three definite components behaves like this. Its components would not take only two values, and a reading along xxx could not erase a reading along zzz. We need a state that holds the probabilities for every direction. We need rules that give those probabilities and the state after a reading, and a rule for the motion of a state in a field. Atoms straight from the oven, before any magnet, are taken up in Lecture 3.

1.2 States are rays

The space of the theory is C2\C^2C2 with the inner product, antilinear in the first slot, ⟨χ,ψ⟩=χ1‾ ψ1+χ2‾ ψ2.\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:inner} \inner{\chi}{\psi}=\overline{\chi_1}\,\psi_1+\overline{\chi_2}\,\psi_2 . \end{equation}⟨χ,ψ⟩=χ1​​ψ1​+χ2​​ψ2​.(1.1) The standard basis is ∣0⟩=(1,0)\ket0=(1,0)∣0⟩=(1,0) and ∣1⟩=(0,1)\ket1=(0,1)∣1⟩=(0,1). In the physicists’ notation a vector ψ\psiψ is written as a ket ∣ψ⟩\ket\psi∣ψ⟩, and the inner product ⟨χ,ψ⟩\inner\chi\psi⟨χ,ψ⟩ is written ⟨χ|ψ⟩\braket\chi\psi⟨χ∣ψ⟩. Here ⟨χ∣\bra\chi⟨χ∣ is a bra, that is, the linear functional ψ↦⟨χ,ψ⟩\psi\mapsto\inner\chi\psiψ↦⟨χ,ψ⟩.

For a unit vector ψ\psiψ, the notation ∣ψ⟩ ⁣⟨ψ∣\proj\psi∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣ means the matrix that sends χ\chiχ to ⟨ψ|χ⟩ψ\braket\psi\chi\psi⟨ψ∣χ⟩ψ. In the physicists’ notation, ∣χ⟩⟼∣ψ⟩ ⁣⟨ψ|χ⟩=⟨ψ|χ⟩∣ψ⟩.\ket\chi\longmapsto\ket\psi\!\braket\psi\chi=\braket\psi\chi\ket\psi .∣χ⟩⟼∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣χ⟩=⟨ψ∣χ⟩∣ψ⟩. It is the orthogonal projection onto the line through ψ\psiψ.

Postulate 1.1 (States). The states of a qubit are described by unit vectors ψ∈C2\psi\in\C^2ψ∈C2. Two unit vectors describe the same state if and only if they differ by a phase, that is, ψ′=eiηψ\psi'=e^{\ii\eta}\psiψ′=eiηψ with η\etaη real. A state of a qubit is a ray [ψ]={eiηψ:η∈R}.[\psi]=\{e^{\ii\eta}\psi:\eta\in\R\}.[ψ]={eiηψ:η∈R}.

A unit vector in C2\C^2C2 is ψ=α∣0⟩+β∣1⟩,where∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1.\psi=\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1,\quad\text{where}\quad\abs\alpha^2+\abs\beta^2=1.ψ=α∣0⟩+β∣1⟩,where∣α∣2+∣β∣2=1. With α=a0+ia1\alpha=a_0+\ii a_1α=a0​+ia1​ and β=b0+ib1\beta=b_0+\ii b_1β=b0​+ib1​ this reads a02+a12+b02+b12=1a_0^2+a_1^2+b_0^2+b_1^2=1a02​+a12​+b02​+b12​=1, so the unit vectors form the three-sphere S3S^3S3 in R4\R^4R4. Each circle {eiηψ}\{e^{\ii\eta}\psi\}{eiηψ} in S3S^3S3 is a single state. A phase must therefore be invisible. The matrix ∣ψ⟩ ⁣⟨ψ∣\proj\psi∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣ does not see it: ∣eiηψ⟩⟨eiηψ∣=eiηe−iη∣ψ⟩ ⁣⟨ψ∣=∣ψ⟩ ⁣⟨ψ∣.\ket{e^{\ii\eta}\psi}\bra{e^{\ii\eta}\psi}=e^{\ii\eta}e^{-\ii\eta}\proj\psi=\proj\psi .​eiηψ⟩⟨eiηψ​=eiηe−iη∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣=∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣. So this matrix depends only on the ray [ψ][\psi][ψ].

Only the phase in front of the whole vector is invisible. The vectors ∣+x⟩=12(∣0⟩+∣1⟩)and∣−x⟩=12(∣0⟩−∣1⟩)\ket{+x}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket0+\ket1\bigr)\quad\text{and}\quad \ket{-x}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\bigl(\ket0-\ket1\bigr)∣+x⟩=2​1​(∣0⟩+∣1⟩)and∣−x⟩=2​1​(∣0⟩−∣1⟩) differ by the sign of one component, yet they are orthogonal. Every state is a superposition α∣0⟩+β∣1⟩\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1α∣0⟩+β∣1⟩ of the two states that the magnet along zzz reads as +1+1+1 and −1-1−1. A superposition is not a state that is sometimes ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩ and sometimes ∣1⟩\ket1∣1⟩. The state ∣+x⟩\ket{+x}∣+x⟩ reads +1+1+1 along xxx with certainty, and neither ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩ nor ∣1⟩\ket1∣1⟩ does.

1.3 The Bloch sphere

The Pauli matrices are σx=(0110),σy=(0−ii0),σz=(100−1).\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\ii\\ \ii&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.σx​=(01​10​),σy​=(0i​−i0​),σz​=(10​0−1​). They are self-adjoint. Multiplying two of them gives the Pauli rule σaσb=δab11+i∑cϵabcσcfor a,b∈{x,y,z},\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:pauli} \sigma_a\sigma_b=\delta_{ab}\Id+\ii\sum_c\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c \qquad\text{for } a,b\in\{x,y,z\}, \end{equation}σa​σb​=δab​11+ic∑​ϵabc​σc​for a,b∈{x,y,z},(1.2) with ϵxyz=1\epsilon_{xyz}=1ϵxyz​=1 and ϵ\epsilonϵ antisymmetric. Hence Tr⁡σa=0\Tr\sigma_a=0Trσa​=0 and Tr⁡(σaσb)=2δab\Tr(\sigma_a\sigma_b)=2\delta_{ab}Tr(σa​σb​)=2δab​. For a vector v∈R3\mathbf v\in\R^3v∈R3 we write v⋅σ=vxσx+vyσy+vzσz\mathbf v\cdot\sigvec=v_x\sigma_x+v_y\sigma_y+v_z\sigma_zv⋅σ=vx​σx​+vy​σy​+vz​σz​.

Definition 1.2 (Bloch vector). The Bloch vector of a unit vector ψ=α∣0⟩+β∣1⟩\psi=\alpha\ket0+\beta\ket1ψ=α∣0⟩+β∣1⟩ is the vector r(ψ)∈R3\blochv(\psi)\in\R^3r(ψ)∈R3 with components ra=⟨ψ,σaψ⟩r_a=\inner{\psi}{\sigma_a\psi}ra​=⟨ψ,σa​ψ⟩. Written out, r(ψ)=(2Re⁡(αˉβ), 2Im⁡(αˉβ), ∣α∣2−∣β∣2).\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:blochcomponents} \blochv(\psi)=\bigl(2\operatorname{Re}(\bar\alpha\beta),\ 2\operatorname{Im}(\bar\alpha\beta),\ \abs\alpha^2-\abs\beta^2\bigr). \end{equation}r(ψ)=(2Re(αˉβ), 2Im(αˉβ), ∣α∣2−∣β∣2).(1.3)

Theorem 1.3 (The Bloch sphere). Let ψ\psiψ and χ\chiχ be unit vectors in C2\C^2C2.

  1. The Bloch vector is a unit vector, ∣r(ψ)∣=1\abs{\blochv(\psi)}=1∣r(ψ)∣=1, and r(eiηψ)=r(ψ)\blochv(e^{\ii\eta}\psi)=\blochv(\psi)r(eiηψ)=r(ψ) for every η∈R\eta\in\Rη∈R.

  2. With r=r(ψ)\blochv=\blochv(\psi)r=r(ψ), ∣ψ⟩ ⁣⟨ψ∣=12(11+r⋅σ).\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:projector} \proj{\psi}=\frac12\bigl(\Id+\blochv\cdot\sigvec\bigr). \end{equation}∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣=21​(11+r⋅σ).(1.4)

  3. Every unit vector r=(sin⁡θcos⁡ϕ,sin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,cos⁡θ)\blochv=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)r=(sinθcosϕ,sinθsinϕ,cosθ) is the Bloch vector of exactly one state, the ray of ψ(θ,ϕ)=cos⁡(θ/2)∣0⟩+eiϕsin⁡(θ/2)∣1⟩.\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:rep} \psi(\theta,\phi)=\cos(\theta/2)\ket0+e^{\ii\phi}\sin(\theta/2)\ket1 . \end{equation}ψ(θ,ϕ)=cos(θ/2)∣0⟩+eiϕsin(θ/2)∣1⟩.(1.5)

  4. The overlap of two states is ∣⟨χ,ψ⟩∣2=12(1+r(χ)⋅r(ψ)).\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:overlap} \abs{\inner{\chi}{\psi}}^2=\frac12\bigl(1+\blochv(\chi)\cdot\blochv(\psi)\bigr). \end{equation}∣⟨χ,ψ⟩∣2=21​(1+r(χ)⋅r(ψ)).(1.6) So χ⊥ψ\chi\perp\psiχ⊥ψ if and only if r(χ)=−r(ψ)\blochv(\chi)=-\blochv(\psi)r(χ)=−r(ψ).

Hence the states of a qubit are the points of the unit sphere, the Bloch sphere.

Proof.

By (1.3), ∣r∣2=4∣α∣2∣β∣2+(∣α∣2−∣β∣2)2=(∣α∣2+∣β∣2)2=1.\abs{\blochv}^2=4\abs\alpha^2\abs\beta^2+\bigl(\abs\alpha^2-\abs\beta^2\bigr)^2 =\bigl(\abs\alpha^2+\abs\beta^2\bigr)^2=1 .∣r∣2=4∣α∣2∣β∣2+(∣α∣2−∣β∣2)2=(∣α∣2+∣β∣2)2=1. 1.4 Observables and measurement

Postulate 1.5 (Observables). Each measurable quantity of a qubit, an observable, is a self-adjoint matrix A=A†A=\adj AA=A† on C2\C^2C2. Its possible readings are its eigenvalues.

Physicists also say Hermitian. This course says self-adjoint. By the spectral theorem (Linear Algebra for Physics, from now on Linear Algebra, Thm 10.10), a self-adjoint AAA is A=∑aa Ea,A=\sum_aa\,E_a,A=a∑​aEa​, where aaa runs over the distinct eigenvalues of AAA, and EaE_aEa​ is the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace ker⁡(A−a11)\ker(A-a\Id)ker(A−a11) of aaa. For a self-adjoint matrix, ∑aEa=11\sum_aE_a=\Id∑a​Ea​=11.

Postulate 1.6 (Measurement). An ideal measurement of an observable AAA on the state [ψ][\psi][ψ] obeys two rules.

  1. Born’s rule. It gives the reading aaa with probability Prob⁡(a)=⟨ψ,Eaψ⟩=∥Eaψ∥2.\Prob(a)=\inner{\psi}{E_a\psi}=\norm{E_a\psi}^2 .Prob(a)=⟨ψ,Ea​ψ⟩=∥Ea​ψ∥2.

  2. Lüders’ rule. If the reading is aaa, which requires Prob⁡(a)>0\Prob(a)>0Prob(a)>0, the state immediately afterwards is the ray [Eaψ∥Eaψ∥].\Bigl[\frac{E_a\psi}{\norm{E_a\psi}}\Bigr].[∥Ea​ψ∥Ea​ψ​].

Both rules depend only on the ray, since a phase in front of ψ\psiψ changes neither the probability ∥Eaψ∥2\norm{E_a\psi}^2∥Ea​ψ∥2 nor the ray of EaψE_a\psiEa​ψ. They are two separate assumptions, and Lüders’ rule does not follow from Born’s rule. The change of state is often called collapse. The postulate predicts what follows a reading, which (F1) and (F3) require. It claims nothing about how, or whether, a physical process brings the change about. Lecture 39 describes more general models of measurement. Lecture 42 asks what can account for one definite result. A reading of probability 000 does not occur, and it has no state after it.

Proposition 1.7 (The observables of a qubit). Every self-adjoint 2×22\times22×2 matrix is A=a11+b m⋅σ,A=a\Id+b\,\mvec\cdot\sigvec,A=a11+bm⋅σ, with a∈Ra\in\Ra∈R, b≥0b\ge0b≥0 and m\mvecm a unit vector.

  1. If b>0b>0b>0, the readings of AAA are a±ba\pm ba±b, with projections E±=12(11±m⋅σ),\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:projections} E_\pm=\frac12\bigl(\Id\pm\mvec\cdot\sigvec\bigr), \end{equation}E±​=21​(11±m⋅σ),(1.7) and E±=∣ψ±⟩ ⁣⟨ψ±∣E_\pm=\proj{\psi_\pm}E±​=∣ψ±​⟩⟨ψ±​∣, where ψ±\psi_\pmψ±​ is the state with Bloch vector ±m\pm\mvec±m.

  2. If b=0b=0b=0, then A=a11A=a\IdA=a11 reads aaa with certainty, and the measurement leaves the state unchanged.

Put a=12(p+q)a=\tfrac12(p+q)a=21​(p+q) and b=(u,v,12(p−q))\mathbf b=(u,v,\tfrac12(p-q))b=(u,v,21​(p−q)).

If b=0\mathbf b=0b=0, then A=a11A=a\IdA=a11. Its only eigenvalue is aaa, with Ea=11E_a=\IdEa​=11, so Prob⁡(a)=1\Prob(a)=1Prob(a)=1 and Lüders’ rule returns the ray of ψ\psiψ.

By the Pauli rule (m⋅σ)2=11(\mvec\cdot\sigvec)^2=\Id(m⋅σ)2=11, so the matrices E±E_\pmE±​ are self-adjoint, with E±2=E±E_\pm^2=E_\pmE±2​=E±​, E+E−=0E_+E_-=0E+​E−​=0 and E++E−=11E_++E_-=\IdE+​+E−​=11. So every observable that is not a multiple of 11\Id11 is a reading along an axis m\mvecm, up to the two numbers it reports.

A Stern–Gerlach magnet along m\mvecm measures ℏ2 m⋅σ\tfrac\hbar2\,\mvec\cdot\sigvec2ℏ​m⋅σ, where ℏ\hbarℏ is Planck’s constant divided by 2π2\pi2π. Its readings ±ℏ2\pm\tfrac\hbar2±2ℏ​ we have recorded as ±1\pm1±1.

Corollary 1.8 (Born’s rule on the sphere). In the state with Bloch vector r\blochvr, a measurement along a unit vector m\mvecm reads ±1\pm1±1 with probabilities Prob⁡(±1)=12(1±m⋅r).\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:born} \Prob(\pm1)=\frac12\bigl(1\pm\mvec\cdot\blochv\bigr). \end{equation}Prob(±1)=21​(1±m⋅r).(1.8) After the reading ±1\pm1±1, the Bloch vector is ±m\pm\mvec±m.

Proof. By the overlap formula (1.6), ⟨ψ,E±ψ⟩=∣⟨ψ±|ψ⟩∣2=12(1±m⋅r).\inner\psi{E_\pm\psi}=\abs{\braket{\psi_\pm}\psi}^2=\frac12(1\pm\mvec\cdot\blochv).⟨ψ,E±​ψ⟩=∣⟨ψ±​∣ψ⟩∣2=21​(1±m⋅r). The vector E±ψ=⟨ψ±|ψ⟩ψ±E_\pm\psi=\braket{\psi_\pm}\psi\psi_\pmE±​ψ=⟨ψ±​∣ψ⟩ψ±​ is a multiple of ψ±\psi_\pmψ±​. When the reading occurs it is nonzero, and its normalisation lies on the ray of ψ±\psi_\pmψ±​. 

Figure 1.4 draws (1.8). A measurement along m\mvecm sees only the component m⋅r\mvec\cdot\blochvm⋅r of the state along its axis, the shadow of r\blochvr on the axis, as it were. The facts of §1.1 follow. After the reading +1+1+1 along zzz, the Bloch vector is ez\mathbf e_zez​, and a second reading along zzz is certain (F1). An axis at angle θ\thetaθ to ez\mathbf e_zez​ has m⋅r=cos⁡θ\mvec\cdot\blochv=\cos\thetam⋅r=cosθ, so Prob⁡(±1)=12(1±cos⁡θ)\Prob(\pm1)=\tfrac12(1\pm\cos\theta)Prob(±1)=21​(1±cosθ), that is, cos⁡2(θ/2)\cos^2(\theta/2)cos2(θ/2) and sin⁡2(θ/2)\sin^2(\theta/2)sin2(θ/2) (F2). After the reading +1+1+1 along xxx, the Bloch vector is ex\mathbf e_xex​, whose component along zzz is 000 (F3). The reading along xxx did not reveal a hidden value along zzz. It replaced the state.

Remark 1.9 (One observable sees one component). All the states on one circle of latitude about m\mvecm, that is, all r\blochvr with the same m⋅r\mvec\cdot\blochvm⋅r, give the same statistics for every observable a11+b m⋅σa\Id+b\,\mvec\cdot\sigveca11+bm⋅σ. Unless the circle is a single pole, a single observable therefore cannot determine the state. Three observables along independent axes can, and Exercise Sheet 1 shows how.

1.5 The Hamiltonian and time evolution

Postulate 1.10 (Evolution). Between measurements, the state vector obeys the Schrödinger equation iℏ dψtdt=Hψt.\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:schrodinger} \ii\hbar\,\frac{\dd\psi_t}{\dd t}=H\psi_t . \end{equation}iℏdtdψt​​=Hψt​.(1.9) Here the Hamiltonian HHH is the observable whose readings are the energies.

Lemma 1.11 (Evolution is unitary). The only solution with ψ0=ψ\psi_0=\psiψ0​=ψ is ψt=Utψ\psi_t=U_t\psiψt​=Ut​ψ, where Ut=e−itH/ℏU_t=e^{-\ii tH/\hbar}Ut​=e−itH/ℏ. For every observable AAA, ddt⟨ψt,Aψt⟩=iℏ⟨ψt,[H,A]ψt⟩,where [H,A]=HA−AH.\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:ehrenfest} \frac{\dd}{\dd t}\inner{\psi_t}{A\psi_t} =\frac{\ii}{\hbar}\inner{\psi_t}{\comm HA\psi_t}, \qquad\text{where }\comm HA=HA-AH . \end{equation}dtd​⟨ψt​,Aψt​⟩=ℏi​⟨ψt​,[H,A]ψt​⟩,where [H,A]=HA−AH.(1.10) In particular, UtU_tUt​ is unitary and maps rays to rays.

Proof. Existence and uniqueness are Linear Algebra, Prop. 6.21, for the matrix −iH/ℏ-\ii H/\hbar−iH/ℏ. Next we differentiate the inner product. A constant leaves the first slot conjugated, so ddt⟨ψt,Aψt⟩=iℏ⟨Hψt,Aψt⟩−iℏ⟨ψt,AHψt⟩.\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\inner{\psi_t}{A\psi_t} =\frac{\ii}{\hbar}\inner{H\psi_t}{A\psi_t}-\frac{\ii}{\hbar}\inner{\psi_t}{AH\psi_t}.dtd​⟨ψt​,Aψt​⟩=ℏi​⟨Hψt​,Aψt​⟩−ℏi​⟨ψt​,AHψt​⟩. Since H=H†H=\adj HH=H†, the first term is iℏ⟨ψt,HAψt⟩\tfrac{\ii}{\hbar}\inner{\psi_t}{HA\psi_t}ℏi​⟨ψt​,HAψt​⟩, which gives (1.10). For A=11A=\IdA=11 the commutator vanishes, so ∥ψt∥\norm{\psi_t}∥ψt​∥ is constant for every initial vector. A matrix that preserves every norm is unitary (Linear Algebra, Thm 9.20). Finally, Ut(eiηψ)=eiηUtψU_t(e^{\ii\eta}\psi)=e^{\ii\eta}U_t\psiUt​(eiηψ)=eiηUt​ψ. 

So HHH must be self-adjoint, or the total probability ∥ψt∥2\norm{\psi_t}^2∥ψt​∥2 would drift. By Proposition 1.7, every Hamiltonian of a qubit is either c11c\Idc11, which moves no state, or H=c11+ℏν2 n⋅σwith ν>0\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:H} H=c\Id+\frac{\hbar\freq}{2}\,\nvec\cdot\sigvec\qquad\text{with } \freq>0 \end{equation}H=c11+2ℏν​n⋅σwith ν>0(1.11) and n\nvecn a unit vector. Its energies are E±=c±12ℏνE_\pm=c\pm\tfrac12\hbar\freqE±​=c±21​ℏν, so ν=(E+−E−)/ℏ\freq=(E_+-E_-)/\hbarν=(E+​−E−​)/ℏ.

Theorem 1.12 (Precession). Under the Hamiltonian (1.11), the Bloch vector of ψt\psi_tψt​ obeys r˙=ν n×r.\begin{equation} \label{eq:1:precession} \dot{\blochv}=\freq\,\nvec\times\blochv . \end{equation}r˙=νn×r.(1.12) Hence r(t)=cos⁡(νt) r0+sin⁡(νt) n×r0+(1−cos⁡νt)(n⋅r0) n.\blochv(t)=\cos(\freq t)\,\blochv_0+\sin(\freq t)\,\nvec\times\blochv_0 +(1-\cos\freq t)(\nvec\cdot\blochv_0)\,\nvec .r(t)=cos(νt)r0​+sin(νt)n×r0​+(1−cosνt)(n⋅r0​)n. The sphere turns rigidly about n\nvecn through the angle νt\freq tνt, anticlockwise when seen from the tip of n\nvecn.

Proof. Put A=σaA=\sigma_aA=σa​ in (1.10). The term c11c\Idc11 commutes with σa\sigma_aσa​. By the Pauli rule, [σb,σa]=2i∑cϵbacσc\comm{\sigma_b}{\sigma_a}=2\ii\sum_c\epsilon_{bac}\sigma_c[σb​,σa​]=2i∑c​ϵbac​σc​, so iℏ[H,σa]=iν2∑bnb[σb,σa]=ν∑b,cϵabc nbσc.\frac{\ii}{\hbar}\comm{H}{\sigma_a} =\frac{\ii\freq}{2}\sum_bn_b\comm{\sigma_b}{\sigma_a} =\freq\sum_{b,c}\epsilon_{abc}\,n_b\sigma_c .ℏi​[H,σa​]=2iν​b∑​nb​[σb​,σa​]=νb,c∑​ϵabc​nb​σc​. Taking ⟨ψt, ⋅ ψt⟩\inner{\psi_t}{\,\cdot\,\psi_t}⟨ψt​,⋅ψt​⟩ of both sides gives r˙a=ν∑b,cϵabcnbrc=ν(n×r)a,\dot r_a=\freq\sum_{b,c}\epsilon_{abc}n_br_c=\freq(\nvec\times\blochv)_a,r˙a​=νb,c∑​ϵabc​nb​rc​=ν(n×r)a​, which is (1.12). This linear equation has exactly one solution with r(0)=r0\blochv(0)=\blochv_0r(0)=r0​ (Linear Algebra, Prop. 6.21). The displayed rotation equals r0\blochv_0r0​ at t=0t=0t=0, and differentiating it with n×(n×r0)=(n⋅r0)n−r0\nvec\times(\nvec\times\blochv_0)=(\nvec\cdot\blochv_0)\nvec-\blochv_0n×(n×r0​)=(n⋅r0​)n−r0​ gives ν n×r(t)\freq\,\nvec\times\blochv(t)νn×r(t). 

The eigenstates of HHH, at r=±n\blochv=\pm\nvecr=±n, do not move. They are the stationary states. The component n⋅r\nvec\cdot\blochvn⋅r is constant, so the energy statistics 12(1±n⋅r)\tfrac12(1\pm\nvec\cdot\blochv)21​(1±n⋅r) of every state are constant, even when the state moves.

A spin in a nonzero uniform magnetic field B\mathbf BB has H=−γ ℏ2 σ⋅B,H=-\gamma\,\frac\hbar2\,\sigvec\cdot\mathbf B,H=−γ2ℏ​σ⋅B, with γ\gammaγ the magnetic moment per unit spin (the gyromagnetic ratio). For γ>0\gamma>0γ>0 this is (1.11) with c=0c=0c=0, n=−B/∣B∣\nvec=-\mathbf B/\abs{\mathbf B}n=−B/∣B∣ and the Larmor frequency ν=γ∣B∣\freq=\gamma\abs{\mathbf B}ν=γ∣B∣.

1.6 A worked sequence

Example 1.13 (Evolve, then measure twice). Figure 1.5 shows this example.

  1. Prepare. The state is ψ0=32∣0⟩+12∣1⟩,r0=(32,0,12),\psi_0=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\ket0+\tfrac12\ket1,\qquad \blochv_0=\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},0,\tfrac12\bigr),ψ0​=23​​∣0⟩+21​∣1⟩,r0​=(23​​,0,21​), which is (1.5) with θ=π/3\theta=\pi/3θ=π/3 and ϕ=0\phi=0ϕ=0.

  2. Evolve. The Hamiltonian and the time are H=ℏν2σzandt∗=π/(2ν),H=\tfrac{\hbar\freq}{2}\sigma_z\quad\text{and}\quad t_*=\pi/(2\freq),H=2ℏν​σz​andt∗​=π/(2ν), a quarter turn. Theorem 1.12 turns the Bloch vector about zzz to r(t∗)=(0,32,12)\blochv(t_*)=\bigl(0,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\tfrac12\bigr)r(t∗​)=(0,23​​,21​).

  3. Read the statistics. Along zzz, Prob⁡(+1)=34\Prob(+1)=\tfrac34Prob(+1)=43​ and Prob⁡(−1)=14\Prob(-1)=\tfrac14Prob(−1)=41​ at every time. Along xxx, Prob⁡(+1)=12(1+32cos⁡(νt)).\Prob(+1)=\frac12\Bigl(1+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\cos(\freq t)\Bigr).Prob(+1)=21​(1+23​​cos(νt)). This is 2+34≈0.933\tfrac{2+\sqrt3}{4}\approx0.93342+3​​≈0.933 at t=0t=0t=0, with 2−34≈0.067\tfrac{2-\sqrt3}{4}\approx0.06742−3​​≈0.067 for −1-1−1, and it is 12\tfrac1221​ at t∗t_*t∗​. The relative phase of ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩ and ∣1⟩\ket1∣1⟩ changes, and the reading along xxx sees it.

  4. Measure xxx, then zzz at once. At t∗t_*t∗​, measure along xxx and suppose the reading is +1+1+1, which has probability 12\tfrac1221​. The state is now ∣+x⟩\ket{+x}∣+x⟩. A second reading along xxx, made at once, is +1+1+1 with certainty. A reading along zzz, made at once, gives ±1\pm1±1 with probability 12\tfrac1221​ each. So “+1+1+1 along xxx, then +1+1+1 along zzz” has probability 12⋅12=14\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac1421​⋅21​=41​. Without the reading along xxx, +1+1+1 along zzz had probability 34\tfrac3443​.

Laboratory

The Bloch sphere: a state that turns, and the act of measurement

Prepare the state ψ(θ0,ϕ0)\psi(\theta_0,\phi_0)ψ(θ0​,ϕ0​), choose the axis n\nvecn of the Hamiltonian H=c11+ℏν2 n⋅σH=c\Id+\tfrac{\hbar\freq}2\,\nvec\cdot\sigvecH=c11+2ℏν​n⋅σ and run the clock: r\blochvr turns about n\nvecn on the circle where n⋅r\nvec\cdot\blochvn⋅r stays fixed, anticlockwise seen from the tip of n\nvecn (Theorem 1.12). Choose a measurement axis m\mvecm: Born'sss rule sees only the component m⋅r\mvec\cdot\blochvm⋅r of r\blochvr along m\mvecm, its shadow on the axis, as it were (Corollary 1.8). Measure once and the state jumps to +m+\mvec+m or −m-\mvec−m; prepare many fresh copies and the frequencies approach 12(1±m⋅r)\tfrac12(1\pm\mvec\cdot\blochv)21​(1±m⋅r). The draws are pseudorandom (seeded, so every run can be replayed): their long-run frequencies match Born'sss probabilities up to a generator bias of order 10−510^{-5}10−5, far below the sampling noise for N≤1000N\le1000N≤1000.     Predict, test, explain

    1.7 A state holds probabilities, not values

    In classical mechanics the state of a particle is its position and its velocity. These fix the value of every observable, such as its energy. A point of the Bloch sphere fixes less. It fixes the reading along m\mvecm only when m=±r\mvec=\pm\blochvm=±r, and along any other axis only its probabilities. Between measurements the point moves on the sphere by a definite law, as a classical state does. But it holds probabilities, not values. Exercise Sheet 1 compares this motion with classical mechanics.

    The qubit, as a quantum system

    States: the rays of C2\C^2C2, which are the points r\blochvr of the Bloch sphere (Postulate 1.1 and Theorem 1.3). Observables: the self-adjoint matrices a11+b m⋅σa\Id+b\,\mvec\cdot\sigveca11+bm⋅σ. Unless b=0b=0b=0, each is a reading along an axis m\mvecm (Postulate 1.5 and Proposition 1.7). Evolution: ψt=e−itH/ℏψ\psi_t=e^{-\ii tH/\hbar}\psiψt​=e−itH/ℏψ. The Hamiltonian H=c11+ℏν2n⋅σH=c\Id+\tfrac{\hbar\freq}2\nvec\cdot\sigvecH=c11+2ℏν​n⋅σ turns the sphere about n\nvecn at the rate ν\freqν (Postulate 1.10 and Theorem 1.12). Measurement: along m\mvecm, the reading is ±1\pm1±1 with probability 12(1±m⋅r)\tfrac12(1\pm\mvec\cdot\blochv)21​(1±m⋅r), and the state afterwards is ±m\pm\mvec±m (Postulate 1.6 and Corollary 1.8).

    Summary

    • The Bloch sphere: states are points, and orthogonal states are antipodal (Theorem 1.3).
    • Born’s rule on the sphere and precession: the statistics of a measurement depend on one component, and a Hamiltonian turns the sphere (Corollary 1.8 and Theorem 1.12). A point of the sphere holds probabilities, not values.

    Lecture 2 drives the qubit with a field that turns in time, and Lecture 3 fills the inside of the sphere.
